slides.title: Common Equations As A Decision Guide
slides.notes: Open Appendix D as a tool for choosing equations, not a memory contest. The useful habit is to attach every identity to its assumptions, its geometric role, and a quick invariant check, so a formula sheet becomes an engineering aid instead of a wall of symbols.

slides.title: Notation Map: Symbol, Code, Invariant
slides.notes: Use the notation map to slow students down before any computation. The same compact product symbol should trigger three questions: what grades are expected, what implementation operation will be called, and what invariant must remain true after the operation has been applied.

slides.title: Product Families Are Grade Filters
slides.notes: Frame the product definitions as filters applied to one geometric product. This makes the table less arbitrary: outer product selects the top grade, contractions select grade differences, and impossible target grades explain why some products vanish without special pleading.

slides.title: Sign Changes Are Small But Expensive
slides.notes: Treat the sign table as a debugging device. Reversion, grade involution, and Clifford conjugation look harmless, but a single wrong sign changes rotor inverses, dual formulas, and sandwich operations. The displayed patterns should be checked before trusting longer derivations.

slides.title: Inverse And Dual Need Preconditions
slides.notes: Emphasize that inverse and dual equations are not universally available commands. A blade must be non-null before inversion is meaningful, and the pseudoscalar must be invertible before duality behaves cleanly. These assumptions are where many elegant derivations become runtime bugs.

slides.title: Operators: Projection, Reflection, Rotor
slides.notes: Present the three operator formulas as a progression from decomposition to motion. Projection and rejection split a vector relative to a blade, reflection flips one component, and a rotor applies an even transformation while preserving norm and orientation constraints.

slides.title: Exponentials Split Into Three Regimes
slides.notes: The exponential cases are best remembered by the square of the generator. Negative square gives circular functions, zero square truncates after the linear term, and positive square gives hyperbolic functions. The regime test is more important than memorizing every Taylor term.

slides.title: Model Equations: Homogeneous And Conformal
slides.notes: Separate model equations from core algebra equations. Homogeneous formulas manage translations and incidence for flat objects, while conformal formulas embed Euclidean points as normalized null objects. The model must be named before the identity can be trusted.

slides.title: Common Pitfalls Checklist
slides.notes: Use the pitfalls slide as a pause point before examples. Most mistakes are not arithmetic mistakes; they are hidden assumption failures. Check grades, invertibility, unit inputs, normalization, and model conventions before interpreting a compact equation as a geometric truth.

slides.title: Checkable Examples From The Notebook
slides.notes: Connect the lecture back to executable artifacts without asking students to inspect files during class. The examples show what a healthy formula record looks like: a symbolic identity, a concrete small case, and a Boolean or numeric invariant that can fail loudly.

slides.title: Formula Sheet Discipline
slides.notes: Close by making the method portable. Students should leave with a personal rule: every reused equation needs a named family, a visible precondition, and one cheap test. That rule makes the appendix useful across rotors, duals, projections, and conformal constructions.
